a: the Well of the Vision
t: A name turned into its meaning
p: The Ge'ez gives the meaning of Beer-lahai-roi, the well where Isaac lived in Genesis.
b: Genesis says Isaac "made his home by Beer-lahai-roi" (Genesis 25:11), a Hebrew name that Hagar gave the well (Genesis 16:14). The Ge'ez does not spell out the Hebrew name. It translates it: "the well of seeing," the Well of the Vision. Charles explains the full Hebrew name as "the well of the living One that seeth me." Jubilees does the same with Beersheba, which becomes "the Well of the Oath" (24:21). Both renderings may go back to the Greek translation that stood between the Hebrew book and the Ge'ez.

a: in the first year of the third week of this jubilee
p: Every event is dated by jubilee, week of years and year. Here: the 43rd jubilee, year 2073 from creation.
b: "This jubilee" is the forty-third, the one in which Abraham died (chapter 23). A jubilee in this book is 49 years, seven "weeks" of seven years. So the first year of the third week is 42 × 49 + 2 × 7 + 1 = year 2073 from creation, the same figure Charles prints in his margin. Isaac stays at the Well of the Vision seven years (24:1), then twenty-one years in Gerar (24:12, "three weeks of years"), as Charles adds up. The book's point is that history runs on God's fixed sevens.

a: a famine took hold of the land
t: Compared with the Bible: the famine comes first
p: Jubilees puts the famine of Genesis 26:1 before the sale of the birthright. Genesis has it after.
b: In Genesis the sale of the birthright (Genesis 25:29–34) comes before the famine that sends Isaac to Gerar (Genesis 26:1). Jubilees swaps them. Charles suggests the author did it "possibly to explain Esau's hunger": Esau comes in starving because the land is in famine. Changes the order of Genesis, but nothing in Genesis is denied.

a: Hand over to me
p: The Ge'ez verb means "give back, return." It renders a Greek word that means both "give back" and "sell."
b: Genesis 25:31 has Jacob say "Sell me your birthright." The Ge'ez verb ʾägbəʾ is a form of "return," so it can sound as if Jacob asks for what is already his. Charles explains why: the Ge'ez follows the Greek apodou, the word the Septuagint (the old Greek Old Testament) uses in Genesis 25:31, which means "give back" and also "sell." So the odd verb is a sign that Jubilees reached Ethiopia through Greek. The Plain English Translation says "hand over," which fits both senses.

a: your birthright, your right as the firstborn
p: The Ge'ez says the same thing two ways. Charles took this as two renderings of one Greek phrase.
b: The Ge'ez reads, word for word, "your seniority of the first birth." Charles saw here "two renderings" of the Greek ta prōtotokia sou, "your birthright": a translator gave one rendering, and another was added beside it. The Plain English Translation keeps both, because both are in VanderKam's text. The birthright was the eldest son's larger share and leading place in the family (Deuteronomy 21:17).

a: and I will give you bread
t: Compared with the Bible: Jacob names his price
p: In Genesis Jacob asks for the birthright first. Here he offers bread and stew in the same breath.
b: Genesis 25:31 has only "Sell me your birthright first, today." Charles notes that the offer of bread and stew is "not in Gen. xxv. 31." Jubilees makes it a plain trade, openly agreed, and then adds an oath (24:5). The story reads less like a trick and more like a fair bargain that Esau freely chose. Goes beyond Genesis.

a: Esau said to himself
t: Compared with the Bible: a thought, not a complaint
p: In Genesis Esau says aloud that he is about to die. Here he thinks it, "in his heart."
b: Genesis 25:32 gives Esau's words to Jacob: "Here I am, about to die. What good to me is a birthright?" In Jubilees he says it "in his heart" and then tells Jacob simply, "I have given it to you." The change shows what Esau really values. It fits the book's steady contrast between the two brothers (25:8; 26:35; 29:18).

a: So Esau despised the birthright
p: The same scene stands behind Hebrews 12:16, which warns the church not to be like Esau.
b: The sentence repeats Genesis 25:34. Hebrews uses the story as a warning: no one should be one who "treats holy things as nothing, as Esau did. In exchange for one meal he sold his own birthright" (Hebrews 12:16). Jubilees and Hebrews agree that Esau, not Jacob, was at fault. Jubilees then gives the name Edom its cause, the red stew, as Genesis 25:30 does.

a: So Jacob became the elder
t: Compared with the Bible: the result is stated
p: Genesis never says Jacob "became the elder." Jubilees says it outright, and says Esau lost his rank.
b: Genesis lets the reader draw the conclusion. Jubilees states it: Jacob is now the elder, and Esau "was brought down from his rank." This prepares for Isaac's blessing in chapter 26, which goes to the one who now holds the elder's place. It also matches the word given to Rebekah, "the elder will serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23), which Paul cites (Romans 9:12). Goes beyond Genesis by naming the outcome.

a: Isaac set out to go down to Egypt
t: Compared with the Bible: Isaac starts for Egypt
p: Genesis has God tell Isaac not to go to Egypt. Jubilees says Isaac had already set out.
b: In Genesis 26:2 the LORD says "Do not go down to Egypt," but the text does not say Isaac had started. Jubilees says he did, and that God's word stopped him at Gerar. Abraham went down to Egypt in a famine (Genesis 12:10); Isaac is kept in the land.

a: Stay as a foreigner in this land
p: Verses 9–11 follow God's words to Isaac in Genesis 26:2–5 almost word for word.
b: God's speech repeats Genesis 26:2–5: stay in the land, I will be with you, I will give you and your offspring all this land, I will keep the oath I swore to Abraham, your offspring will be like the stars. The Plain English Translation uses the wording of the site's Genesis wherever the Ge'ez says the same thing. The promise itself goes back to Genesis 12:1–3 and Genesis 22:16–18.

a: In your offspring all the nations of the earth will be blessed
p: The Ge'ez has a plain passive, "will be blessed." Genesis 26:4's Hebrew is often read "bless themselves."
b: The site's Genesis 26:4 reads "will bless themselves by your offspring," following the Hebrew verb form. The Ge'ez of Jubilees has a simple passive: the nations "will be blessed" in Isaac's offspring. The New Testament quotes the promise the same way: "In your offspring all the clans of the earth will be blessed" (Acts 3:25), and Paul, "All the nations will be blessed in you" (Galatians 3:8). The difference matters: "bless themselves" can mean only that people will use Abraham's name in blessings; "be blessed" means they will receive the blessing.

a: kept what I required of him
t: Compared with the Bible: Abraham kept God's laws
p: Genesis 26:5 already says Abraham kept God's commands and laws. Jubilees adds "my covenant."
b: Genesis 26:5 says Abraham "kept what I required of him: my commands, my rules and my laws." That verse suits Jubilees perfectly, because the whole book teaches that the patriarchs knew and kept God's laws before Sinai, from the heavenly tablets. The Ge'ez list adds "my ordinances and my covenant." Matches Genesis, with a small addition. Paul reads Abraham differently: he was counted righteous by faith before he was circumcised and before the law (Romans 4:9–13; Galatians 3:17).
orig: ወዐቀበ ዑቃቤየ ወትእዛዛትየ ወሕገጊየ ወሥርዓትየ ወኪዳንየ (wäʿäqäbä ʿuqabeyä wätʾəzazatyä wäḥgägiyä wäśrəʿatyä wäkidanyä)

a: Any man who touches him or anything of his
t: Compared with the Bible: no lie about Rebekah
p: Jubilees leaves out the story in which Isaac calls Rebekah his sister (Genesis 26:6–11).
b: In Genesis, Abimelech's order protects Isaac and his wife after Isaac has lied that Rebekah is his sister (Genesis 26:7–11). Charles points out that Jubilees makes "no reference" to the lie. Here the order protects Isaac and "anything of his." The author often drops what would shame the fathers (compare Abraham's similar lie in Genesis 12:10–20). Charles also mentions the view that "my sister" in 27:14 is meant to soften the omitted story. Leaves out part of Genesis.

a: Hardship
p: Genesis names the wells Esek ("quarrel"), Sitnah ("hostility") and Rehoboth ("wide spaces").
b: The Ge'ez gives the names in translation, as it did with the Well of the Vision. ʿƎṣub means "hard, difficult," and the reason uses the same root: "they made things hard for us." Genesis 26:20 has Esek, "quarrel." Charles notes that the Septuagint has adikia, "injustice," here. The "us" slips into the speech of Isaac's men without warning, in VanderKam's text and in Charles's English alike.
orig: ዕጹብ እስመ ተዐጸቡ ምስሌነ (ʿəṣub ʾəsmä täʿäṣäbu məslenä)

a: he named it Wide
p: Isaac's third well has a name that means "wide," like Rehoboth in Genesis 26:22.
b: Genesis 26:22: "He called it Rehoboth and said, 'For now the LORD has given us room, and we will bear fruit in the land.'" The Ge'ez səfuḥ, "wide," and the verb that follows, "has made wide," keep the same play on words. "Wide" in a land of quarrels is a picture of God's gift of space (compare Psalm 18:19).

a: on the first day of the first month
t: God appears on New Year's Day
p: The Ge'ez says "at the rising of the first month." In Jubilees' fixed calendar that is New Year's Day.
b: Genesis 26:24 says only "that night." Jubilees dates the vision to the first day of the first month. The Ge'ez śärq means the "rising" or beginning of a month. Older English says "new moon," but Jubilees counts a year of 364 days by the sun, not by the moon (6:32–38), so the Plain English Translation says "first day." The book dates many key moments to the four days that open the year's quarters (6:23): Jacob's dream at Bethel also falls on this day (27:19).

a: the one his father Abraham had built first
t: Compared with the Bible: Abraham's altar
p: Genesis says Isaac built an altar at Beersheba. Jubilees says it was the altar Abraham had built first.
b: Genesis 26:25: "There he built an altar and called on the LORD's name." Genesis says Abraham planted a tamarisk at Beersheba and called on the LORD there (Genesis 21:33), but it does not mention an altar. Jubilees links the son's worship to the father's: Isaac restores Abraham's altar as he restores Abraham's wells (24:18). Goes beyond Genesis.

a: and did not find water
t: Compared with the Bible: no water after the treaty
p: Genesis 26:32 says the servants found water. Jubilees says they did not, because of Isaac's oath.
b: In the Hebrew of Genesis 26:32 the servants say, "We have found water." Charles explains that the Hebrew words for "to him" and "not" sound alike (lo), and that the Septuagint and Jubilees read the "not." Jubilees makes a lesson of it: Isaac swore peace with the Philistines (24:26), the well came up dry, and Isaac knew that day he had sworn "under pressure" (24:27). The next verses curse the Philistines. The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's Ge'ez. Conflicts with the Hebrew Genesis.

a: the Well of the Oath
p: Beersheba means "well of the oath" or "well of seven." Jubilees translates the name.
b: In Hebrew beʾer is "well" and shevaʿ is "seven" or "oath." Genesis explains the name twice: Abraham's oath with Abimelech (Genesis 21:31) and Isaac's well Shibah (Genesis 26:33). Jubilees uses "the Well of the Oath" for Beersheba throughout (27:19; 29:17–19), so the place keeps reminding the reader of the oath Isaac came to regret.

a: he had sworn to them under pressure
t: Compared with the Bible: a forced peace
p: Genesis 26 ends in friendship. Jubilees says Isaac learned the treaty had been forced on him.
b: In Genesis 26:28–31 Abimelech, Ahuzzath and Phicol come asking for a covenant because "the LORD has been with you," and the two sides part "in peace." Jubilees leaves the feast and the friendly words out and has Isaac realize the oath was forced. That turns the treaty into a reason for the curse in 24:28–33. Conflicts with the tone of Genesis.

a: Cursed are the Philistines
t: Why so fierce? The Maccabean wars
p: Charles argued that this curse makes sense only in the 100s BC, when the Maccabees fought the Philistine cities.
b: Nothing in Genesis prepares for this curse. Charles thought it "hardly intelligible save in a contemporary of the wars waged by the Maccabeans against the Philistine cities." He lists what 1 Maccabees reports: Ashdod (Azotus in 1 Maccabees) plundered by Judas (1 Maccabees 5:68), Ashdod burned with the temple of Dagon by Jonathan (1 Maccabees 10:84), Ekron given to Jonathan (1 Maccabees 10:89), Gaza forced to surrender (1 Maccabees 11:61–62). If he is right, the curse put in Isaac's mouth is also a word for the book's first readers, who saw those wars. Charles concluded that the passage reflects "the attitude of Judah towards the cities of the Philistines in the second cent. B.C."

a: the Kittim
p: A name from Genesis 10:4 for people of Cyprus and the Greek west. Charles takes it here as the Macedonians.
b: The Kittim are sons of Javan in Genesis 10:4, a people usually linked with Cyprus. The name came to mean powers from over the sea: "Ships will come from the coast of Kittim" (Numbers 24:24). Charles notes that the Kittim are the Romans in Daniel 11:30 but the Macedonians in 1 Maccabees 1:1, and he takes them here as the Macedonians, since Alexander the Great captured Gaza. The Qumran commentaries also speak of the Kittim (see the topic on the pesharim).

a: the righteous people
p: Charles reads this as Judah under the Maccabees, the nation the author hoped would finish the work.
b: Isaac's curse looks ahead to a "righteous people" who root out the Philistines who escape other enemies. Charles's note: "Judah under the Maccabees." Read as prophecy, the verse gives Israel a role in God's judgment; read historically, it blesses wars the author knew. Both readings agree that the author wanted his people to see their struggles as part of God's plan.

a: Caphtorim
p: The Bible says the Philistines came from Caphtor (Amos 9:7; Deuteronomy 2:23).
b: Amos speaks of "the Philistines from Caphtor" (Amos 9:7), and Jeremiah calls them "the remnant of the island of Caphtor" (Jeremiah 47:4). Deuteronomy says the Caphtorim "came from Caphtor" and settled near Gaza (Deuteronomy 2:23). Charles cites these verses, and for where Caphtor lay he refers to "the various views" in the Encyclopaedia Biblica. Charles also notes that the Ge'ez has "all Caphtorim," which he corrected with the Latin to "these Caphtorim." Jubilees uses the old name to stress that the Philistines are outsiders in the land.

a: Even if he goes up to the sky
p: Charles shows that verses 31–32 are built on Amos 9:2–4. Psalm 139 uses the same pictures for comfort.
b: Amos says of Israel's sinners: "Even if they tunnel down to Sheol" (Amos 9:2), God's hand will pull them out, and if they go into captivity the sword will find them there (Amos 9:4). Jubilees turns that word against the Philistines: sky, earth, the nations, Sheol and captivity give no escape. Psalm 139:8 uses the same places to say that God is near to those he loves. Obadiah 4 says the same of proud Edom.

a: there his condemnation will be great
t: Compared with the Bible: punishment in Sheol
p: In most of the Hebrew Bible Sheol is simply the grave. Here the wicked are condemned even there.
b: Sheol is the realm of the dead. In most of the Old Testament all the dead go there and little is said of reward or punishment (Psalm 6:5; Ecclesiastes 9:10). Jubilees speaks of condemnation in Sheol and of "a curse that lasts forever" (24:32), closer to 1 Enoch 22, where the dead are kept apart by their deeds, and to Jesus' parable in Luke 16:23. Goes beyond most of the Hebrew Bible, in a direction the New Testament also takes.

a: written and engraved about him on the heavenly tablets
t: A curse on the heavenly tablets
p: The heavenly tablets hold not only laws but judgments on peoples, fixed before they happen.
b: The heavenly tablets (ṣəlatä sämay; see the note at 3:10) appear often in this part of the book: for laws (28:6; 30:9), for a man's righteousness (30:19–20), for Isaac's blessing of Levi and Judah (31:32), and here for a judgment on the Philistines. "Engraved" stresses that it cannot be changed. The idea is that God's decisions are already written in heaven, and history carries them out.

a: do not take a wife for yourself from the daughters of Canaan
t: Compared with the Bible: Rebekah speaks first
p: Genesis gives this warning to Isaac (Genesis 28:1). Jubilees gives it to Rebekah, before the stolen blessing.
b: In Genesis, Rebekah complains about the Hittite women (Genesis 27:46) and Isaac then tells Jacob not to marry a Canaanite (Genesis 28:1–2). Charles observes that Jubilees moves this charge before Genesis 27 and puts it in Rebekah's mouth. So before any blessing is given, Jacob has already proved himself the son who will keep the family line pure. Isaac still repeats the charge later (27:9–10). Changes the order and the speaker.

a: He took two wives from the offspring of Canaan
p: Genesis names them: Judith and Basemath, daughters of Hittites. They grieved Isaac and Rebekah.
b: Genesis 26:34 says Esau at forty married "Judith, Beeri the Hittite's daughter, and Basemath, Elon the Hittite's daughter," and "They were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and to Rebekah" (Genesis 26:35). Jubilees counts the Hittites among the "offspring of Canaan," as Genesis 10:15 makes Heth a son of Canaan. Rebekah's words "they have made my soul bitter" echo Genesis 26:35.

a: All their deeds are sexual immorality and lust
t: Compared with the Bible: the charge against Canaan's women
p: Genesis says Esau's wives grieved his parents. Jubilees says their whole way of life was immoral.
b: Genesis gives no reason why Esau's wives were "a bitterness of spirit." Jubilees supplies one: unclean deeds, sexual immorality and lust, "no righteousness in them at all." The charge matches the book's fierce teaching against marriage with the nations (30:7–17). The Torah links marriage with Canaanites to the worship of their gods (Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3–4). Goes beyond Genesis.

a: your offspring will be holy
p: Rebekah's hope uses the language Ezra later uses for Israel's pure line: "the holy seed."
b: The Ge'ez says "your seed will be holy." Ezra grieved that "the holy seed has mingled with the peoples of the lands" (Ezra 9:2), and Malachi 2:15 speaks of God seeking "Offspring from God." Jubilees reads Jacob's marriage as the first test of that holiness. Rebekah calls Jacob "a pure son and a holy offspring" (25:12). For how churches apply such texts to marriage today, see the cards at Ezra 10 and 2 Corinthians 6.

a: I am nine weeks of years old
p: Nine weeks of years is 63. Genesis Rabbah also makes Jacob 63 at the blessing, though Jubilees 45:13 implies another age.
b: Nine "weeks" of seven years make 63 years. Charles quotes a rabbinic parallel from Genesis Rabbah 68: "Our father Jacob was sixty-three years old when he received the blessing." The same passage goes on to make Jacob eighty-four when he married. Charles also points out a conflict inside Jubilees: sixty-three years here put Jacob's birth in the year 2046 from creation, but 45:13 puts it in 2041. He adds that Esau was then 63 too, and that Esau married at 40 (Genesis 26:34), so the "twenty-two years" of 25:8 fit. Charles also notes that Syncellus, a Byzantine chronicler, "wrongly attributes" Jacob's words about never knowing a woman to Josephus.

a: I have not known any woman or touched one
t: Compared with the Bible: Jacob's chastity
p: Genesis says nothing of Jacob's life before he left home. Jubilees makes him a model of self-control.
b: Jubilees gives Jacob a speech that Genesis does not have: he has not been with a woman, has not been engaged, and refuses a Canaanite bride. He has guarded his spirit because Abraham warned him about lust and sexual immorality (25:7). For the book's first readers, Jacob is the young man who stays pure when his brother does not. Goes beyond Genesis.

a: the words of Abraham our father
p: Jacob recalls Abraham's warning in Jubilees 22:20 not to marry from the offspring of Canaan.
b: In Jubilees 22:20 Abraham tells Jacob to beware of taking a wife from the offspring of Canaan's daughters, because Canaan's offspring is to be rooted out. Genesis has a similar charge from Abraham about Isaac's bride (Genesis 24:3–4). Jubilees has Jacob hear it from his grandfather himself, whose life overlaps his in this book.

a: marry a sister of my two wives
t: Compared with the Bible: Esau pressures Jacob
p: Genesis does not say Esau urged Jacob to marry a Canaanite. Jubilees adds 22 years of pressure.
b: Jubilees invents nothing new in the facts of Genesis, but it adds a scene: for twenty-two years Esau has kept pushing Jacob to marry one of his wives' sisters. The detail makes the brothers opposites: one marries outside the family, the other refuses. Goes beyond Genesis.

a: spread out the fingers of her hands
t: A woman who prays and blesses
p: Raised hands were the usual posture of prayer. Rebekah prays and then blesses like a patriarch.
b: People in the Bible prayed standing with hands spread toward heaven (Exodus 9:29; 1 Kings 8:22; Psalm 28:2). Rebekah first blesses God (25:11–13) and then lays both hands on Jacob's head and blesses him (25:14–23). Genesis gives only fathers such blessings. Jubilees gives the mother a full blessing, and Isaac later shows the same honor to her (27:14–18).

a: came down into her mouth
p: A spirit comes down into Rebekah's mouth, as a spirit of prophecy later comes into Isaac's (31:12).
b: Jubilees treats Rebekah as one who speaks by God's Spirit. The same thing is said of Isaac before he blesses Levi and Judah (31:12). Charles points out that later Jewish tradition also gave Rebekah prophetic knowledge: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 27:42 says Esau's words were told to her "by the Holy Spirit," and Genesis Rabbah calls her a prophetess. Jubilees itself says Esau's plan was told to her in a dream (27:1).

a: Blessed are you, righteous Lord, God of the ages
p: Rebekah blesses God, then turns to bless her son.
b: The poem begins by blessing God and then speaks to Jacob ("May he bless you"). The change of person is in the Ge'ez and is kept. The themes of verses 15–22, many sons, the land, God dwelling among them, blessing for those who bless, gather up the promises of Genesis 12, 15 and 28.
orig: ቡሩክ አንተ እግዚኦ ጻድቅ አምላኮሙ ለዓለማት (buruk ʾäntä ʾəgziʾo ṣadq ʾämlakomu läʿalämat)

a: as many as the months of the year
p: There are twelve months in the year and twelve sons of Jacob. Rebekah's blessing foretells the twelve tribes.
b: Rebekah prays that Jacob's sons may "arise as many as the months of the year," that is, twelve. Chapter 28 then records the births of eleven of them, and Benjamin follows in chapter 32.

a: as he said he would give it to Abraham and to his offspring after him for all time
p: Charles compares Mary's song: "to Abraham and his offspring for all time" (Luke 1:55).
b: Mary ends her song with God's mercy "as he told our fathers he would, / to Abraham and his offspring for all time" (Luke 1:55). Charles noticed that both Luke and Jubilees add the phrase as an aside, and that Luke "recalls both Mic. vii. 20 and our text." The likeness shows a shared Jewish way of speaking about the promise. Whether Luke knew Jubilees cannot be shown.

a: My tender love and my breasts bless you
p: The Ge'ez word for "tender love" is also "mercy." Womb and breasts bless the son they bore and fed.
b: The Ge'ez məḥrät means "mercy, compassion," and the Hebrew word for compassion is related to "womb." Charles suspected "my affection" was a doubled translation of "womb" and bracketed it; VanderKam keeps it, and so does the Plain English Translation. The line about "the woman who bore you" in VanderKam's Ge'ez says "in her lifetime" (with an odd spelling); Charles corrected his manuscripts' "my" to "thy." Compare Jacob's own blessing of "breasts and womb" (Genesis 49:25).

a: may his sanctuary be built by them for all the ages
p: Rebekah looks ahead to the temple, built by Jacob's descendants, as the book's first chapter does.
b: The hope that God will "live among" Israel and that his sanctuary will stand among them recalls Exodus 25:8 and Ezekiel 37:26–28. Charles points to Jubilees 1:29, where the sanctuary of the Lord is promised for all time. For the book's first readers in the 100s BC the temple in Jerusalem was standing; the prayer asks that it last forever.

a: Whoever blesses you, blessed!
p: The closing words repeat the promise to Abraham and Isaac's blessing of Jacob.
b: God told Abraham, "I will bless those who bless you" (Genesis 12:3). Isaac's blessing ends "Whoever curses you, cursed! / Whoever blesses you, blessed!" (Genesis 27:29), and Balaam repeats it (Numbers 24:9). Jubilees gives the same words to Rebekah, and again to Isaac (26:24; 31:17, 20). Rebekah adds "falsely": only an unjust curse falls back on the one who speaks it.

a: May the Lord of the world love you
p: Charles compares Sirach 4:10, where God "will love you with more love than your own mother has."
b: The last line compares God's love with a mother's. Charles points to Sirach 4:10, which tells the one who protects orphans and widows, "he will love you with more love than your own mother has" (Sirach 4:10). Isaiah also compares God's love to a mother's (Isaiah 49:15; Isaiah 66:13). "Lord of the world" (ʾƎgziʾä ʿaläm) can also be rendered "Lord of eternity."

a: Isaac called Esau, his older son
p: Chapter 26 follows Genesis 27:1–41 closely. The changes all protect Jacob or darken Esau.
b: The scene keeps Genesis's order and much of its wording: the hunt, Rebekah's plan, the goatskins, the blessing, Esau's cry, the lesser word for Esau, the threat. The Plain English Translation follows the site's Genesis where the Ge'ez says the same. The changes are telling: Jacob never says "I am Esau" (26:13, 19), heaven itself blinds Isaac (26:18), Esau's future is a "sin that is wholly for death" (26:34), and Esau wishes for his father's death (26:35).

a: I will not hold back anything my father eats that pleases him
t: Compared with the Bible: the dutiful son
p: Genesis has Jacob object at once that Esau is hairy. Jubilees first has him stress his care for his father.
b: Charles notes that the first half of this verse is "added by our author in favour of Jacob." Before Jacob voices his fear of being found out, he says he would gladly give his father anything he likes to eat. The same concern for Isaac returns when Jacob refuses to leave his old father without his consent (27:6). Goes beyond Genesis.

a: I am your son
t: Compared with the Bible: Jacob avoids the lie
p: In Genesis Jacob says "It is I, Esau, your firstborn." In Jubilees he says only "I am your son."
b: Genesis 27:19 has Jacob say plainly, "It is I, Esau, your firstborn," and later, asked "Are you really my son Esau?", answer "I am" (Genesis 27:24). Jubilees changes both answers to "I am your son" (26:13, 19), which is true. Charles cites a similar rescue in Genesis Rabbah 65, where Rabbi Levi takes Jacob's words to mean "I am he who will receive the ten commandments (which begin with the words 'I am'), but Esau is thy first born." Both show Jewish readers uneasy with Jacob's deceit. Changes Genesis.

a: heaven had turned events so as to take away his power to perceive
p: Charles traced this clause to 1 Kings 12:15, where the LORD "had brought about this turn."
b: Jubilees says Isaac failed to recognize Jacob because heaven took away his discernment, literally "made his spirit pass." Charles saw the wording as borrowed from 1 Kings 12:15: "The LORD had brought about this turn." The Ge'ez miṭät means a "turn" or "dispensation." So the blessing reached Jacob by God's will, not only by Rebekah's plan. Paul also sees God's choice at work: "not by works but by the one who calls" (Romans 9:11).

a: from the dew of the sky and from the dew of the earth
p: Genesis 27:28 says "richness of the earth." The Ge'ez says "dew of the earth," like the Ethiopic Genesis.
b: The site's Genesis 27:28 reads "some of the dew of the sky / and some of the richness of the earth." The Ge'ez of Jubilees has "dew" twice. Charles notes that "the same rendering" of the Greek "richness of the earth" is found in the Ethiopic version of Genesis 27:28, so the translator of Jubilees used the same wording as the Ethiopian Bible. The Ge'ez also adds "make you many" and "may he give you," which Charles cut as extra words but VanderKam keeps. Wheat and oil stand for the harvest of the land.
orig: እምጠለ ሰማይ ወእምጠለ ምድር (ʾəmṭälä sämay wäʾməṭälä mədr)

a: May all the blessings with which the Lord blessed me
p: Isaac adds the blessing of Abraham, which Genesis gives only later, when Jacob leaves home (Genesis 28:4).
b: In Genesis 27 Isaac's blessing is about plenty and rule. The blessing of Abraham, the land and the many offspring, comes in Genesis 28:4: "May he give you Abraham's blessing." Charles notes the link. Jubilees joins the two, so that the stolen blessing already carries the covenant promise. The closing "Whoever curses you, cursed!" repeats Genesis 27:29.

a: he hid
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez says Jacob hid as Esau came in. Charles thought the words were added and marked them.
b: The Ge'ez täḫäbʾä, "he hid himself," stands in VanderKam's text and is kept in the Plain English Translation. Charles marked "he hid himself and" as doubtful and suggested reading simply "that Esau came in," as in Genesis 27:30. Read as it stands, it pictures Jacob slipping away just in time.

a: Isaac was utterly astonished
p: Genesis 27:33 says Isaac shook with a great trembling. The Ge'ez says he was astonished.
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 27:33 says Isaac "trembled a great trembling," and the site renders "Isaac shook with a great trembling, past all measure." The Ge'ez tädämä dəmamä means "was amazed with an amazement." Isaac's words then confirm the blessing: "He will be blessed, he and all his offspring forever." Jubilees adds "all his offspring," making the blessing reach Israel.
orig: ወተደመ ይስሐቅ ድማመ ዐቢየ ጥቀ (wätädämä yəsḥäq dəmamä ʿäbiyä ṭəqä)

a: Now I know why he was named Jacob
p: Esau plays on Jacob's name: he has "tripped me up" twice. Charles suspected a slip in the Greek.
b: In Genesis 27:36 Esau says, "Isn't that why he is named Jacob? He has grabbed me by the heel these two times." The Hebrew name Yaʿaqov sounds like ʿaqev, "heel," and the verb "trip up, cheat." The Ge'ez ʾäʿqäṣäni keeps a similar sound. Charles thought "now I know why" might come from a Greek "how" that was a slip for "rightly," which would match Genesis.

a: Isaac answered him
t: Verse 33 in the Ge'ez used here
p: The transcription of VanderKam's Ge'ez used here runs 26:32-33 together. The division follows Charles.
b: The transcription of VanderKam's Ge'ez used here runs 26:32-33 together; the division follows Charles. In that transcription Esau's weeping and Isaac's answer, "Look, from the dew of the earth your home will be, and from the dew of the sky above," stand inside the verse numbered 32, and no verse is numbered 33. Charles begins verse 33 with "And Esau lifted up his voice and wept," and the Plain English Translation does the same, so that references to Jubilees 26:33 find the same words here as in Charles. Nothing is missing: the Ge'ez has the whole answer.

a: away from the dew of the earth
p: The Ge'ez "from" can mean "some of" or "away from," exactly as in the Hebrew of Genesis 27:39.
b: Genesis 27:39 uses the Hebrew min, "from," which can mean "some of" (as in 27:28, a blessing) or "away from" (a loss). The site renders "away from," and so does Charles ("far from"). The Ge'ez ʾəm has the same double sense. In Jubilees the harsh reading fits what follows: Esau will sin unto death (26:34).
orig: እምጠለ ምድር ይኩን ንብረትከ (ʾəmṭälä mədr yəkun nəbrätkä)

a: then you will commit a sin that is wholly for death
t: Compared with the Bible: Esau's doom
p: Genesis promises Esau will one day break Jacob's yoke. Jubilees says he will then sin unto death.
b: Genesis 27:40 ends: "But when you break loose, / you will tear his yoke off your neck." Jubilees turns this into a curse: when Esau throws off the yoke, he will commit a sin "wholly for death" and his offspring will be uprooted. Charles calls the change "contrary to all tradition": the Targum Onkelos says Esau will remove the yoke when Jacob's sons break the law. Syncellus quotes the Jubilees form as if it were Genesis, in Greek: plēmmelēsēs eis thanaton, "you will offend unto death." The book later tells of Esau's war on Jacob (chapters 37–38). Conflicts with Genesis 27:40.
orig: ትኤብስ አበሳ ኵሎ ለሞት (təʾebs ʾäbäsa kʷəlo lämot)

a: Now let the days of mourning for my father come
t: Compared with the Bible: Esau wishes for his father's death
p: In Genesis Esau waits for his father's death before taking revenge. In Jubilees he wishes it would come.
b: Genesis 27:41: "The days of mourning for my father are drawing near. Then I will kill Jacob my brother." Charles calls Jubilees' wording a "malicious turn" given to Esau's words: Esau wants the days of mourning to come now. Jubilees also says he "kept threatening" Jacob. Changes Genesis to darken Esau.

a: was told to Rebekah in a dream
t: Compared with the Bible: a dream reveals Esau's plan
p: Genesis says only that "someone told Rebekah." Jubilees says it came to her in a dream.
b: Genesis 27:42 leaves the messenger unnamed. Jubilees makes the warning a revelation in a dream. Charles notes that Targum Pseudo-Jonathan says Esau's words were told to her "by the Holy Spirit," and that Genesis Rabbah calls Rebekah a prophetess. In Jubilees God keeps guiding Rebekah, as in her blessing of Jacob (25:14). Goes beyond Genesis.

a: take revenge on you
p: Genesis 27:42 says Esau is "comforting himself" with the thought of killing. The Ge'ez says he plans revenge.
b: The site's Genesis 27:42: "Esau your brother is comforting himself with the thought of killing you." The Ge'ez yətqeyämäkä means "takes vengeance on you." The Hebrew verb behind "comfort himself" can also mean to ease one's anger by revenge, and the Ge'ez gives that sense outright.

a: If he wants to kill me, I will kill him
t: Compared with the Bible: Jacob is not afraid
p: Genesis never has Jacob speak of fighting Esau. Jubilees has him ready to, and later he does (chapter 38).
b: In Genesis Jacob flees without a word. Jubilees gives him courage, and Rebekah's answer, "Do not let me be robbed of both my sons in one day," comes from Genesis 27:45. The threat looks ahead: in Jubilees 38:2 Jacob shoots Esau with an arrow when Esau makes war on him. The quiet man of Genesis 25:27 becomes a warrior. Goes beyond Genesis.

a: If I leave him, it will be wrong in his eyes
t: Jacob will not abandon his father
p: Charles, following Singer, saw this verse as a defense of Jacob against a charge known from later Jewish tradition.
b: Jacob refuses to go unless Isaac sends him. Charles cites the scholar Singer: in rabbinic tradition Jacob was blamed for staying away from his parents so long (Megillah 16b), while Esau was praised as a model son (Genesis Rabbah 65 and 82). Jubilees answers the charge in advance: Jacob left only when his father sent him, and he later sent gifts four times a year (29:15–20). Honoring parents is the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12).

a: I am sick of my life because of the two daughters of Heth
p: Rebekah's words come from Genesis 27:46, where she gives Isaac a reason to send Jacob away.
b: Genesis 27:46: "I am sick of living because of the daughters of Heth." Genesis lets the reader see that Rebekah wanted Jacob out of Esau's reach. Jubilees makes her plan open: Jacob refuses to go without his father's word (27:6), so Rebekah goes in and gets it (27:7–8). The marriage question and the danger from Esau are joined.

a: Mesopotamia
p: Where Genesis 28:2 has Paddan-aram, the Ge'ez has Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers.
b: The site's Genesis 28:2 sends Jacob "to Paddan-aram," the Hebrew name for the region around Haran in upper Mesopotamia. The Ge'ez mäsp̣eṭomya is the Greek name "Mesopotamia," "between the rivers," a sign of the Greek stage of the text. Stephen also says Abraham was "in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran" (Acts 7:2).

a: God Almighty
p: The Ge'ez keeps the Hebrew word Shaddai: ʾämlakä säday, "God Shaddai," as in Genesis 28:3.
b: Genesis 28:3 begins Isaac's blessing "May God Almighty bless you," Hebrew El Shaddai. The Ge'ez writes ʾämlakä säday, keeping Shaddai as a name. "Almighty" is the traditional English. The blessing then follows Genesis 28:3–4: a gathering of nations, Abraham's blessing, the land where Jacob is a foreigner. Where Genesis says "God gave," the Ge'ez says "the Lord gave."

a: Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean
p: The Ge'ez says "the Syrian." "Syrian" is the Greek name for the people Genesis calls Arameans.
b: The Ge'ez soryawi means "Syrian." Genesis 28:5 calls Laban "the Aramean." The Arameans lived in the lands the Greeks called Syria, so the two words name the same people. The Plain English Translation uses the site's "Aramean," as in Genesis.

a: My sister
p: Isaac calls his wife "my sister." Charles shows this was a tender way to address a wife.
b: Charles notes that "my sister" is "an expression of tenderness." Tobit calls his wife "sister" (Tobit 5:21), and the lover in the Song of Songs calls his bride "my sister, my bride" (Song of Songs 4:9). He adds Singer's suggestion that the author also meant to explain why Isaac called Rebekah his sister in Gerar, the episode Jubilees leaves out (see 24:13). The scene shows a tender Isaac and Rebekah in agreement.

a: He is a blameless man
p: Genesis 25:27 calls Jacob tam, "quiet." The same Hebrew word means "blameless" in Job 1:1.
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 25:27 calls Jacob ish tam, which the site renders "a quiet man." The word tam also means "blameless, whole," as of Job (Job 1:1). The Ge'ez fəṣum means "perfect, complete." Jubilees reads Jacob's character in the moral sense: upright, blameless, faithful. That is how the book wants Jacob seen, in spite of the stolen blessing.
orig: ወፍጹም ውእቱ ብእሲ ምእመን ውእቱ (wäfṣum wəʾtu bəʾsi məʾmän wəʾtu)

a: Luz on the mountain, that is, Bethel
p: Bethel ("house of God") was first called Luz (Genesis 28:19). Jacob arrives on New Year's Day.
b: Genesis says Jacob named the place Bethel, "though the city was called Luz before that" (Genesis 28:19). Jubilees dates the night to the first day of the first month, the same day God appeared to Isaac at the Well of the Oath (24:22). Bethel becomes important in this part of the book: Jacob returns there to pay his vow (31:1–3), and in chapter 32 Levi is made priest there.

a: under that tree
p: Genesis does not mention a tree. Charles wondered if it was a sacred pole at a Canaanite shrine.
b: Genesis 28:11 says Jacob took one of the stones and lay down. Jubilees adds that he set it "under that tree," as if the tree were well known. Charles notes the phrase is "not found in Gen. xxviii. 11" and suggests it may be the wooden pole (Asherah) that stood at Canaanite places of worship. Genesis 35:8 mentions an oak below Bethel. The Latin, as Charles reports it, adds "at his head" here.

a: a stairway
p: The Ge'ez word comes from "go up": a way up. Older English says "ladder"; the site's Genesis says "stairway."
b: The Ge'ez mäʿarg is formed from ʿärgä, "go up," and means a means of going up. The Hebrew sullam of Genesis 28:12 appears only there; the site renders it "stairway," and the Plain English Translation follows. Jubilees says "the angels of the Lord" where Genesis says "angels of God." Jesus takes up the scene: "you will see heaven standing open, and God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man" (John 1:51).

a: the Lord was standing on it
t: On the stairway, or beside Jacob?
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 28:13 can mean "above it" or "beside him." The Ge'ez says "on it."
b: The Hebrew ʿalav in Genesis 28:13 can mean "on it, above it" (the stairway) or "beside him" (Jacob). The site's Genesis says "stood above it." The Ge'ez wəsteta, "on it," takes the first sense: the Lord stands at the top of the stairway that joins earth and heaven.

a: like the sand of the earth
p: Genesis 28:14 says "dust of the earth." The Ge'ez says "sand," as in God's word to Isaac (24:22).
b: The site's Genesis 28:14 reads "Your offspring will be like the dust of the earth." The Ge'ez has ḫoṣa, "sand," which also appears in 24:22. Both pictures, dust and sand, say the same: too many to count (Genesis 13:16; Genesis 22:17).

a: Truly this place is the house of the Lord
t: Compared with the Bible: the house of the Lord
p: In Genesis Jacob says "The LORD really is in this place." In Jubilees: "this place is the house of the Lord."
b: Genesis 28:16: "The LORD really is in this place, and I did not know it." Jubilees has Jacob say at once that the place is "the house of the Lord," the meaning of the name Bethel, and it repeats "house of the Lord" where Genesis 28:17 has "house of God." The book is interested in where God may be worshiped: in chapter 32 an angel tells Jacob not to build a sanctuary at Bethel. Changes the wording slightly.

a: Jacob made a vow
p: The Ge'ez says Jacob "prayed a prayer." The same Ge'ez words stand for a vow in this book.
b: The Ge'ez reads ṣäläyä yaʿqob ṣälotä, "Jacob prayed a prayer," where Genesis 28:20 has "made a vow." The context makes it a vow, and Charles translates "vowed a vow." The same words return when Jacob goes to Bethel to pay what he promised (31:1, 26, 29), and in 31:31 for Isaac's blessing, which is called a "prayer." The Plain English Translation says "vow" where the sense is a promise, and "prayer" in 31:31.

a: I will give a tenth to you, my God
p: Jacob vows a tenth, as in Genesis 28:22. Jubilees tells how he paid it, through Levi, in chapter 32.
b: Genesis 28:22 ends with "of everything you give me I will give a tenth, a tenth to you." Abraham had already given Melchizedek "a tenth of everything" (Genesis 14:20). In Jubilees 32 Jacob pays the vow at Bethel, giving a tenth of all he has, and Levi is set apart as the "tenth" of his sons (Charles's notes on 32:2–3). This part prepares for that scene: Jacob comes to Bethel to make his offering (31:3, 26–29).

a: He picked up his feet
p: Chapter 28 compresses Genesis 29:1–31:2: the marriages, eleven births and the flocks.
b: The opening words match Genesis 29:1, "Jacob picked up his feet." Jubilees skips the meeting at the well and the month with Laban (Genesis 29:2–14) and goes straight to the seven years of service. A "week" is a week of years: seven years (Genesis 29:20). The births are listed with exact dates (28:11–24), and the story of the flocks is told without Jacob's peeled branches (28:27–28).

a: Zilpah
p: The Ge'ez names are Zalafa and Balan. The Plain English Translation uses the familiar English forms.
b: The Ge'ez spells the slave women's names Zäläfa (here) and Balan (28:9), as Charles notes. These are forms of Zilpah and Bilhah in Genesis 29:24 and 29:29, and the Plain English Translation uses the familiar forms. Jubilees adds that Bilhah was Zilpah's sister (28:9).

a: Leah's eyes were weak, but her form was very beautiful
t: Compared with the Bible: Leah's beauty
p: Genesis says Leah's eyes were "soft." Jubilees adds that she was very beautiful in form.
b: The site's Genesis 29:17 reads "Leah's eyes were soft, but Rachel was lovely in form and lovely to look at." The Hebrew rakkot may mean "tender" or "weak." The Ge'ez says "weak," but then adds that Leah too was very beautiful. Charles notes that Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and Genesis Rabbah 70 explain Leah's weak eyes by her weeping. Jubilees honors Leah, mother of Levi and Judah.

a: It is not right to do this
p: Laban's custom becomes a law of heaven. Charles: these are the angel's words, and the law is unknown elsewhere.
b: Laban gives his reason in Genesis 29:26: "It is not done this way in our place." Then the voice changes. Charles notes, with Singer, that "these are the words of the angels enunciating the law": the angel tells Moses that the heavenly tablets forbid giving a younger daughter in marriage before an older one. Charles adds that, according to Beer and Singer, "there is no hint" of this rule in Jewish tradition. Jubilees often finds a law of heaven behind a story in Genesis.

a: they bring up guilt against him in heaven
p: The Ge'ez says "they make guilt go up about him into heaven," that is, record it there.
b: The verb yaʿärgu, "they bring up," is the same word used for recording deeds on the heavenly tablets in 30:19–20 and 31:32. Angels write down guilt (here) and righteousness (30:17–23). The picture of heavenly books of deeds also appears in Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 20:12.
orig: አበሳ ያዐርጉ በእንቲአሁ ውስተ ሰማይ (ʾäbäsa yaʿärgu bäʾnətiʾähu wəstä sämay)

a: command the Israelites not to do this thing
t: Compared with the Bible: a law Moses never gave
p: No law of Moses requires an older daughter to marry first. And Leviticus forbids marrying two sisters at once.
b: The angel tells Moses to command Israel to marry off the older daughter first. The Torah contains no such law. Charles adds that Jacob's marriage to two sisters was "expressly forbidden by the later law": "Do not take a woman as a rival to her sister... while her sister is still alive" (Leviticus 18:18). He also cites Justin Martyr, who says such a marriage is not lawful (Dialogue with Trypho 134). Jubilees, so strict elsewhere, says nothing about the problem. Goes beyond the Bible, and sits uneasily with Leviticus 18:18.

a: Let the seven days of this one's feast pass
p: A wedding feast lasted seven days. Jacob received Rachel after Leah's week, not after seven more years.
b: Genesis 29:27–28: "Finish this one's wedding week, and we will give you the other one too." Samson's wedding feast also lasts seven days (Judges 14:12, 17). Charles points out that Jubilees "rightly understands" Genesis: Jacob married Rachel a week after Leah, and then served seven more years.

a: Bilhah, Zilpah's sister
p: Genesis does not say Bilhah and Zilpah were sisters. Other Jewish writings do.
b: Charles notes that the Testament of Naphtali also makes Bilhah and Zilpah sisters, daughters of a man named Rotheus, who was a brother of Deborah, Rebekah's nurse. Later Jewish tradition (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 29:24, 29; Genesis Rabbah 74) made them daughters of Laban by a concubine. So Jacob's four wives were two pairs of sisters. Genesis says only that Laban gave each daughter a slave woman (Genesis 29:24, 29).

a: he named him Reuben
p: Genesis says Leah named her sons. VanderKam's Ge'ez says "he named him" for several of them.
b: In Genesis 29:32–35 Leah names Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah, each with a reason. VanderKam's Ge'ez has the masculine "he called" at 28:11, 13, 14, 15, 18 and 22, and the feminine "she called" for Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Zebulun and Joseph. Charles's own text has "she called" from verse 19 to 24, Issachar (28:22) included (see the variant there), and he suggested reading "she called" at 11, 13, 14, 15 and 18 as well. The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam. Jubilees also drops the reasons for the names that Genesis gives, except for Levi's, which comes later (31:16).

a: Leah was hated
p: The Ge'ez and the Hebrew say "hated." In family law the word means the less-loved wife.
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 29:31 says Leah was senuʾah, "hated." The site renders "the unloved one," because the word is used of the wife a man loves less (Deuteronomy 21:15: "one loved and the other unloved"). The Ge'ez also says "hated." The same contrast of "loved" and "hated" is used of Jacob and Esau in Malachi 1:2–3 and Romans 9:13.

a: Have I kept the fruit of your womb from you?
t: Compared with the Bible: no angry Jacob
p: In Genesis Jacob answers Rachel in anger: "Am I in the place of God?" Jubilees removes the anger.
b: Genesis 30:2: "Jacob's anger flared against Rachel, and he said, 'Am I in the place of God, who has kept the fruit of the womb from you?'" Jubilees keeps the question about "the fruit of your womb" but drops the anger and the mention of God, and adds "Have I abandoned you?" Jacob sounds hurt, not harsh. Changes Genesis.

a: in the sixth year of the third week
p: Taken as written, the dates put Dan's birth before Judah's. Charles judged several of them corrupt.
b: Every birth in this chapter has a day, month, year and week. As they stand, Dan (sixth year of the third week) is born before Judah (first year of the fourth week, 28:15), though Bilhah was given to Jacob only after Judah's birth (28:17). Charles called the dates "corrupt" and reported Rönsch's corrections. He also notes that Midrash Tadshe, a later Hebrew work "partly based on our text," gives the same day and month for several births. The chapter page has a table.

a: she too was jealous of Rachel
t: Leah's jealousy: only in the Ge'ez
p: The Ge'ez says Leah too was jealous of Rachel. The Latin and Genesis do not say so.
b: Genesis 30:9: "When Leah saw that she had stopped having children, she took Zilpah her slave woman and gave her to Jacob as a wife." VanderKam's Ge'ez adds that Leah "too was jealous of Rachel," which would match Rachel's jealousy of Leah in 28:16 and Genesis 30:1. But the words are not secure. The Latin has only "and she gave," and Charles says the text here "is doubtful" (see the variant). If the Ge'ez is right, the author paired the sisters' jealousy; if the Latin is right, Jubilees keeps to Genesis.

a: And she gave him to a nurse
t: Compared with the Bible: no mandrakes
p: Jubilees leaves out the mandrakes (Genesis 30:14–18) and adds that Leah gave Issachar to a nurse.
b: In Genesis Leah buys a night with Jacob for her son's mandrakes, and names Issachar ("wages") for it (Genesis 30:14–18). Jubilees omits the whole bargain, as it omits most of the women's rivalry. Instead it adds a short note that Leah gave Issachar to a nurse. The book does not say why. Leaves out part of Genesis.

a: She conceived and bore two, a son and a daughter
t: Compared with the Bible: Zebulun and Dinah as twins
p: Genesis says Dinah was born "afterward." Jubilees makes Zebulun and Dinah twins born the same day.
b: Genesis 30:19–21 tells of Zebulun's birth, then "Afterward she bore a daughter and named her Dinah." Jubilees has both born on the same day, the seventh of the seventh month. Dinah's age matters for the story of chapter 30, where she is "a little girl, twelve years old" (30:2). Goes beyond Genesis.

a: The Lord was kind to Rachel
p: Genesis 30:22–24: God remembered Rachel. Jubilees dates Joseph's birth to a day that opens a quarter of the year.
b: Genesis says "God remembered Rachel" and she named her son Joseph, praying for another (Genesis 30:22–24). Jubilees says "the Lord was kind," and dates the birth to the first day of the fourth month, one of the four memorial days of 6:23. Charles notes that the book's later dates (34:10; 46:1–3) would require Joseph to be born two years earlier than this.

a: dark and spotted and white
p: Genesis 30:32 has speckled, spotted and dark animals. Charles thought "white" was a mistaken translation.
b: In Genesis 30:32 Jacob asks for "every speckled and spotted sheep, every dark lamb, and the spotted and speckled goats." Charles explains that the Ge'ez "white" renders a Greek word for "speckled with white" and should be translated "speckled," as the same slip appears in the Ethiopic Genesis 30:39. The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's Ge'ez.

a: All the sheep gave birth to spotted young
t: Compared with the Bible: no peeled branches
p: Genesis tells how Jacob bred the flocks with peeled branches. Jubilees leaves the method out.
b: In Genesis 30:37–43 Jacob sets peeled branches before the mating animals and breeds the strong ones for himself. Later he says God gave him the flock (Genesis 31:9–12). Jubilees omits the branches altogether: the flocks simply give birth to marked young, and they go to Jacob. Charles notes that the colors in this verse match the Septuagint of Genesis 30:39. Leaves out Genesis's account, and lets God's gift stand alone.

a: Laban went to shear his sheep
p: Chapter 29 covers Genesis 31:3–33:20 in a few verses: the escape, the covenant, the meeting with Esau.
b: Genesis 31:19 says Laban "had gone to shear his sheep." Jubilees uses that absence for Jacob's escape, and says the flocks were three days away (compare Genesis 30:36; 31:22). It leaves out Rachel's theft of the household gods here; they appear only when Jacob destroys them (31:2). It leaves out Laban's search of the tents, Jacob's long complaint (Genesis 31:36–42) and the night at the Jabbok.

a: spoke to their hearts
p: The Ge'ez idiom means to speak kindly and persuasively, as in Genesis 34:3.
b: The Ge'ez tänagärä wəstä ləbon, "spoke into their heart," is the idiom the site's Genesis 34:3 renders "spoke to the girl's heart," and Isaiah 40:2 uses for speaking tenderly. In Genesis 31:4–16 Jacob gives Rachel and Leah a long speech; here he simply wins them over, and they answer as one: "We will go with you to every place you go," a line that recalls Ruth 1:16.

a: Jacob hid his plan from Laban
p: Genesis 31:20 says Jacob "stole the heart" of Laban. The Ge'ez says he "hid his heart" from him.
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 31:20 says Jacob "stole the heart of Laban the Aramean," an idiom for deceiving him. The Ge'ez says Jacob "hid his heart," that is, kept his plan secret. Charles notes that the Septuagint ("hid") and the Targum Onkelos read the verse the same way. The softer wording fits Jubilees' steady defense of Jacob. The Plain English Translation says "hid his plan."

a: in the third month, on the thirteenth day
p: Jacob leaves on the 21st of the first month; Laban overtakes him on the 13th of the third.
b: Genesis 31:22–23 says Laban heard on the third day and chased Jacob for seven days. Jubilees gives calendar dates instead: Jacob sets out on the twenty-first of the first month, Laban catches him on the thirteenth of the third month, and the covenant meal is on the fifteenth (29:7). Charles notes that "the fifteenth" means the fifteenth of the third month.

a: he appeared to him in a dream at night
p: Genesis 31:24: God came to Laban in a dream. Jubilees says only that the Lord did not let him harm Jacob.
b: In Genesis 31:24 God tells Laban, "Watch yourself. Do not speak with Jacob, whether good or bad," and Laban repeats the warning in Genesis 31:29. Jubilees keeps the dream and its purpose and leaves the long quarrel out. It names God as "the Lord," as the Ge'ez always does.

a: On the fifteenth of those days Jacob made a feast for Laban
t: Claude's theory: a covenant on the Feast of Weeks
p: The meal falls on the 15th of the third month, the date of the Feast of Weeks in Jubilees. That may be deliberate.
b: This is Claude's theory. In Jubilees the Feast of Weeks, the feast of firstfruits, falls in the third month, "in the middle of the month" (15:1; 16:13), and the book says it was kept "to renew the covenant every year" (6:17). Jacob and Laban swear their covenant on the fifteenth of the third month (29:5, 7). If the date is deliberate, the author has placed this covenant on the covenant feast, as he places other covenants and oaths there. Charles notes only that the date is the fifteenth of the third month; I have not found the link discussed in the sources opened for this part.

a: the Heap of Witness
p: Genesis gives the heap a Hebrew name, Galeed, and an Aramaic one. Jubilees translates the meaning.
b: In Genesis 31:47 "Laban named it Jegar-sahadutha; Jacob named it Galeed," Aramaic and Hebrew for "heap of witness." Jubilees gives only the meaning, and leaves out the second name Mizpah and the standing stone (Genesis 31:45–52). The heap marks a border that neither side may cross "with evil intent" (29:7).

a: the land of the Rephaim
t: The Rephaim, the giants of the east
p: The Bible calls the old giant peoples of Bashan and Gilead the Rephaim. Jubilees says they were 10 to 15 feet tall.
b: Genesis 14:5 has Chedorlaomer strike "the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim." Deuteronomy says Og of Bashan was the last of the Rephaim (Deuteronomy 3:11), and "People also counted them as Rephaim, like the Anakim" (Deuteronomy 2:11). Jubilees gives their heights: ten cubits down to seven, roughly fifteen down to ten and a half feet, if a cubit is about eighteen inches. The book ties them to the giants born before the Flood (chapters 5 and 7).

a: Karnaim and Ashtaroth, Edrei, Misur and Beon
t: The cities of the Rephaim and the Maccabees
p: Charles thought these towns were named because Judas Maccabee had recently fought there.
b: Ashtaroth and Edrei were cities of Og (Deuteronomy 1:4; Joshua 12:4). Genesis 14:5 joins Ashteroth and Karnaim as one name; Charles notes that the Syriac and some Septuagint copies have two, as here. Misur may be the "plain" (mishor) of Deuteronomy 3:10, and Beon the Baal-meon of Numbers 32:3. Charles argued that the author named these places because of the Maccabean campaigns: Judas took Karnaim (Carnaim in 1 Maccabees 5:43–44) and destroyed the people of Baean (1 Maccabees 5:4–5).

a: Today there is no people that has done all their sins in full
t: The full measure of the Amorites' sin
p: God told Abraham "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16). Jubilees says it became full.
b: In Genesis 15:16 God tells Abraham his offspring will return in the fourth generation, "for the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full." Jubilees says the Amorites who took the Rephaim's place were "evil and sinful," that no people "today" has sinned as fully, and that they no longer have long life on the earth. Charles read "today" as the writer's own day, after Judas's campaigns.

a: they made peace with each other
t: Compared with the Bible: no wrestling at the Jabbok
p: Genesis 32–33 tells of Jacob's fear, prayer, wrestling, new name and gifts. Jubilees says only that they made peace.
b: Genesis gives two chapters to Jacob's return: his prayer (Genesis 32:9–12), the gifts for Esau, the night at the Jabbok when he wrestles until dawn and is named Israel (Genesis 32:22–32), and the meeting when Esau runs to embrace him (Genesis 33:4). Jubilees keeps one sentence. The name Israel is not given here (Jubilees 32 gives it at Bethel, following Genesis 35:10). Charles notes that the Latin has "Jacob and his eleven sons crossed," like Genesis 32:22. Leaves out most of Genesis 32–33.

a: Jacob lived in booths
p: The Ge'ez word means booths or huts. Genesis 33:17 says Jacob built shelters at a place named Succoth, "booths."
b: The Ge'ez məṣlalat means booths, huts or tents. Genesis 33:17 says Jacob "built himself a house there and made shelters for his livestock. That is why the place is named Succoth." Succoth is the Hebrew word for booths, the same word as in the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:42–43). Jubilees keeps the booths and drops the place name.

a: Beth-shan, to Dothan
p: The places run from the Dead Sea north to Beth-shan and Dothan, and south to the Scorpion Pass.
b: Beth-shan lay where the Jezreel Valley meets the Jordan (1 Samuel 31:10); Dothan is where Joseph found his brothers (Genesis 37:17); Akrabbim, "scorpions," is the pass on Judah's southern border (Numbers 34:4, the site's "Scorpion Pass"). Charles linked Akrabbim with Akrabattene (1 Maccabees 5:3), which he describes as "a district in Idumea, where Judas fought against the Edomites." Beth-shan, he says, was linked with Judas only peacefully, as 2 Maccabees 12:29–31 tells it. The phrase "the Salt Sea" follows the Latin; see the variant.

a: He sent his father Isaac some of all his possessions
t: Compared with the Bible: the good son provides
p: Genesis does not say Jacob supported his parents. Jubilees has him send food four times a year.
b: Jacob sends clothing, food, meat, drink, milk, oil, cheese and dates to Isaac, and gifts to Rebekah four times a year (29:16, 20). Meanwhile Esau has taken his father's flocks and left him alone (29:18). Charles notes the contrast with Esau "who robs his father." The book answers the charge that Jacob neglected his parents (see 27:6). Goes beyond Genesis.

a: four times a year
p: Charles reports Rönsch's guess that the four times match the four "days of remembrance" of 6:23.
b: Jubilees names four turning points: "between the turns of the months," between plowing and harvest, between autumn and the rains, and between winter and spring. Charles reports Rönsch's suggestion that they match the four memorial days Noah set at the start of each quarter, the first day of the first, fourth, seventh and tenth months (6:23). Charles also explains the rains as the early rain of autumn and the late rain of spring, as in the Latin.

a: to Abraham's tower
p: The Ge'ez says Isaac lived in Abraham's "tower" on the mountain of Hebron.
b: The Ge'ez maḫfäd means a tower or a strong upper building. Genesis says Jacob came to Isaac "at Mamre, at Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had lived as foreigners" (Genesis 35:27). Jubilees pictures a fixed home. In 31:6 Rebekah comes out of the tower to meet Jacob.

a: Esau took as his wife Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael
t: Esau's third wife and his move to Seir
p: Genesis 28:9: Esau married Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael. Jubilees adds that he took his father's flocks.
b: Genesis 28:9 says Esau "went to Ishmael and took Mahalath daughter of Ishmael." Genesis 36:3 names Ishmael's daughter Basemath. Genesis 36:6–8 says Esau later moved to Seir because the land could not hold both brothers' herds. Jubilees makes the move an act of greed: Esau gathered "all his father's flocks" and left Isaac alone. Goes beyond Genesis.

a: with all their heart and with all their soul
p: The parents bless Jacob with the words Israel uses for loving God (Deuteronomy 6:5).
b: The phrase recalls the great command: "Love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your being and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:5). Isaac and Rebekah bless Jacob with their whole selves. The next time the family meets, Isaac will bless Jacob's sons Levi and Judah (31:13–20).

a: to Salem, east of Shechem, in peace
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 33:18 can mean "came safely" or "came to Salem." Jubilees has both.
b: The Hebrew shalem in Genesis 33:18 can be an adjective, "safe, whole" (the site: "came safely to the city of Shechem"), or a place name, Salem. Charles notes that the Septuagint, the Syriac, Eusebius and Jerome took it as a place name, and the Samaritan text reads shalom, "in peace." Jubilees "combines both interpretations": Jacob went "to Salem ... in peace." This Salem near Shechem is not the Salem of Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18).
orig: ሳሌምሃ ዘመንገለ ጽባሒሁ ለሰዊማ በሰላም (salemha zämängälä ṣəbaḥihu läsäwima bäsälam)

a: There they carried Dinah, Jacob's daughter, off
t: Compared with the Bible: Dinah is taken
p: Genesis says Dinah "went out to look at the daughters of the land." Jubilees says she was carried off.
b: Genesis 34:1–2 begins with Dinah going out, then Shechem "took her and lay with her and dishonored her." Jubilees leaves out her going out and says "they" carried her off into Shechem's house. Charles notes that the book "makes the whole people share" in the wrong, which helps explain why all the men of the city are punished (30:4–6). Dinah carries no blame. Changes Genesis.

a: She was a little girl, twelve years old
p: Jubilees makes Dinah twelve. Charles notes the Testament of Levi agrees. The book's own dates make her younger.
b: Genesis does not give Dinah's age. Jubilees says she was "a little girl, twelve years old," which makes Shechem's act worse. Charles notes that the Testament of Levi 12 agrees: Levi, six years older, was eighteen. Yet by the book's own dates Dinah was born in the sixth year of the fourth week of the forty-fourth jubilee (28:23), year 2134, and this happened in the first year of the sixth week (30:1), year 2143, which would make her nine. Charles's margin gives the same two years.

a: They spoke with them with evil intent, deceived them and tricked them
t: Compared with the Bible: no circumcision
p: Genesis says Jacob's sons tricked Shechem into being circumcised. Jubilees leaves the circumcision out.
b: In Genesis 34:13–24 the brothers demand that every male in Shechem be circumcised, and on the third day, "while they were in pain," Simeon and Levi kill them (Genesis 34:25). Charles observes that the author "omits all reference to the circumcision of the Shechemites." He could hardly approve of killing men who had accepted circumcision. Charles cites the Testament of Levi 6, where Jacob is angry and grieved "because they had received circumcision and after that were killed." Leaves out the heart of Genesis 34.

a: Simeon and Levi came into Shechem without warning
p: Genesis 34:25–26 tells the same slaughter. Jacob's last words curse it (Genesis 49:5–7). Jubilees praises it.
b: In Genesis 34:25–26 Simeon and Levi "took his sword" and "killed every male," including Hamor and Shechem. Jacob rebukes them (Genesis 34:30), and on his deathbed he says, "Their anger be cursed, for it was savage" (Genesis 49:7). Jubilees calls their deed "judgment" (30:4–5) and Levi's zeal "righteousness" (30:17–18). The next notes trace how far it goes.

a: judgment was decreed in heaven against them
t: Praised or cursed? Readings of Shechem
p: Jubilees says heaven decreed the killing. Other writings of the time agree; Genesis 49 and later rabbis do not.
b: Charles shows that in the two centuries before Christ the deed was "highly extolled." In the Testament of Levi 5 an angel commands Levi to take vengeance on Shechem, and Levi says he did it "as it is written in the tablets of heaven." Judith prays to "God of my ancestor Simeon! You put a sword in his hand to take vengeance on the foreigners who violated a virgin's womb to defile her" (Judith 9:2). Charles adds Philo's praise of the brothers. But Jacob's blessing condemns their anger (Genesis 49:5–7), and Charles notes that later rabbis judged them by it: Genesis Rabbah 98 traces the poverty of Simeon's tribe to that curse.
r: Genesis 49:5–7; Judith 9:2–4; Testament of Levi 5–7; Genesis Rabbah 98

a: he must surely die. They are to stone him with stones
t: Compared with the Bible: death for marrying out
p: No law of Moses puts a father to death for giving his daughter to a Gentile. Jubilees builds one from other laws.
b: Charles notes that this law "does not agree quite with any in the O.T." He traces its parts: stoning is the penalty for giving a child to Molech (Leviticus 20:2: "The people of the land are to stone him with stones"), and Jubilees treats marrying a daughter to a Gentile as giving her to Molech (30:10). Burning the woman recalls Judah's sentence on Tamar (Genesis 38:24) and the law for a priest's daughter who becomes a prostitute: "She is to be burned in fire" (Leviticus 21:9). Goes beyond the Torah: no law of Moses puts to death an Israelite woman who marries a Gentile; Jubilees borrows the burning from Genesis 38:24 and Leviticus 21:9.

a: for Israel is holy to the Lord
p: Israel's holiness is the reason given for every rule in this chapter, as in Deuteronomy 7:6.
b: Deuteronomy gives the reason for not intermarrying with the nations of Canaan: "For you are a people holy to the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 7:6). At Sinai God called Israel "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6), and Jeremiah says "Israel was a holy thing for the LORD" (Jeremiah 2:3). Peter applies the words of Exodus 19:6 to the church (1 Peter 2:9). Jubilees draws the line of holiness at marriage.

a: he has given some of his offspring to Molech
t: Marrying out as giving a child to Molech
p: Jubilees reads Leviticus 18:21 as a ban on marrying a child to a Gentile. The Mishnah later forbade that reading.
b: Leviticus 18:21 says, "Do not hand over any of your children to make them pass over to Molech." Charles shows that Jubilees reads this as giving a child in marriage to a Gentile, and that Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on that verse does the same. The Mishnah (Megillah 4:9) rejects it: whoever translates the verse that way is to be silenced. So the reading was known and disputed among Jews. Charles adds that the Latin has "to a foreigner" where the Ge'ez has "to Molech," an explanation rather than the text.

a: not to give any of their daughters to the nations
p: The command repeats Deuteronomy 7:3. Ezra and Nehemiah enforced it after the exile.
b: Deuteronomy 7:3: "Do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take their daughters for your sons." There the ban concerns the nations of Canaan and is grounded in the danger of idolatry (Deuteronomy 7:4). Ezra and Nehemiah applied it after the exile (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27). Jubilees extends it to every nation and calls it "detestable." On how churches read these commands for Christian marriage today, see the "Where Christians differ" cards at Ezra 10 and 2 Corinthians 6.

a: I wrote for you in the words of the law
p: The angel says he wrote the story of Dinah into the law for Moses. The quoted words change "sister" to "daughter."
b: Jubilees claims that the angel of the presence wrote the stories of Genesis "in the words of the law," for Moses to learn from. The brothers' words come from Genesis 34:14: "give our sister to a man who has a foreskin. That would be a disgrace for us." Jubilees changes "sister" to "daughter," turning the story into a rule for fathers. In Genesis the brothers speak these words as part of their trick.

a: if he shuts his eyes to those who commit uncleanness
t: One man's sin and the whole people
p: The verse builds on the Molech law of Leviticus 20:3–5, but widens the guilt to the whole nation.
b: Leviticus 20:4–5 warns that if the people "look the other way" when a man gives a child to Molech, God will set his face against that man "and against his clan." Charles notes that "shuts his eyes" is the phrase of Leviticus 20:4, and that Jubilees widens the guilt from the clan to "the whole people," to justify Simeon and Levi in killing every man in Shechem. Defiling the sanctuary and profaning God's holy name come from Leviticus 20:3.

a: no receiving from his hand of fruit, offerings, burnt offerings
p: God will not accept the offerings of a people that allows this. The prophets say the same of unjust worship.
b: The Ge'ez lists firstfruits, offerings, burnt offerings, fat and the pleasing smell of sacrifice, none of which God will accept. Malachi says the same of priests who despise God: "An offering from your hands I will not accept" (Malachi 1:10). "Favoritism" (literally "lifting the face") means that no one's rank will excuse him (Deuteronomy 10:17).

a: It was counted to them as righteousness
t: Counted as righteousness: Phinehas and Abraham
p: The words recall Phinehas, whose zeal "was reckoned to him as righteousness" (Psalm 106:31), and Abraham.
b: When Phinehas killed an Israelite and a Midianite woman, "It was reckoned to him as righteousness, / for generation after generation, for all time" (Psalm 106:31), and God gave him "a covenant of priesthood for all time, because he was zealous for his God" (Numbers 25:13). Jubilees uses the same pattern for Levi: zeal against a marriage with outsiders, righteousness counted, priesthood given (30:18). The phrase first described Abraham's faith (Genesis 15:6), as Paul stresses (Romans 4:3). Here it describes an act of violence.

a: The offspring of Levi were chosen for the priesthood
t: Compared with the Bible: why Levi became priest
p: In the Torah the Levites are set apart at Sinai. Jubilees says Levi was chosen for his zeal at Shechem.
b: In Exodus the Levites are set apart after the golden calf, when they kill the idolaters: "Fill your hands today for the LORD" (Exodus 32:29); Moses' blessing praises Levi's faithfulness (Deuteronomy 33:8–11), and Malachi speaks of God's "covenant with Levi" (Malachi 2:4). Genesis, by contrast, has Jacob curse Levi's anger at Shechem (Genesis 49:5–7). Charles notes that Jubilees itself gives a second reason in 32:3, Levi as Jacob's tenth son, and that the Testament of Levi gives yet another. Goes beyond, and stands against Genesis 49.

a: to serve before the Lord as we do, always
p: The angel says Levi's line will serve before the Lord "as we do": priests on earth mirror angels in heaven.
b: The speaker is the angel of the presence. The angels serve before God in heaven, and the priests will serve before him on earth. Isaac's blessing says the same: Levi's sons will serve "like the angels of the presence and like the holy ones" (31:14). Hebrews compares the earthly sanctuary to a copy of the heavenly one (Hebrews 8:5).

a: as a friend and a righteous man
p: Levi is written down as a friend of God, as Abraham was (19:9). James says Abraham "was called the friend of God."
b: Jubilees uses the title "friend" for those whose faithfulness is recorded in heaven: Abraham (19:9), Levi here, and all Israel if they keep the covenant (30:21). Scripture calls Abraham God's friend (Isaiah 41:8; 2 Chronicles 20:7), and James writes that "he was called the friend of God" (James 2:23). Jesus tells his disciples, "I have called you friends" (John 15:15).

a: the book of the living
p: Names can be wiped out of "the book of the living" and written in a book of the destroyed.
b: The Ge'ez mäṣḥäfä ḥəyawan means "the book of the living ones." The Bible speaks of God's book from which names may be wiped (Exodus 32:32–33) and prays, "Let them be wiped out of the scroll of life" (Psalm 69:28). Revelation promises the one who wins, "I will never erase his name from the book of life" (Revelation 3:5). Charles thought the book here might mean the list of those who enjoy blessings in this life. The Latin, as he reports it, calls the second book "the book of destructions."

a: They captured everything that was in Shechem
t: Compared with the Bible: no captive women and children
p: Genesis 34:29 says the brothers carried off the women and children. Jubilees lists only goods and animals.
b: Genesis 34:28–29 lists the flocks, herds and donkeys, and then "All their wealth, all their little children and their wives they carried off as captives." Jubilees keeps the animals and goods and leaves out the captive women and children. The book does not say why. Leaves out part of Genesis.

a: He spoke with them about their having killed the city
t: Spoke with them, or rebuked them?
p: Genesis gives Jacob's rebuke and the brothers' reply. Jubilees says only that he "spoke with them."
b: In Genesis 34:30–31 Jacob says, "You have stirred up trouble for me," and the brothers answer, "Like a prostitute, is that how he should treat our sister?" Jubilees reports neither speech. Charles argued that the Greek translator misread a Hebrew phrase that means "spoke against" as "spoke to," so the original said Jacob "reproached them." VanderKam's Ge'ez says "spoke with them," and the Plain English Translation keeps that. Either way, Jubilees gives Jacob fear of the Canaanites, not moral outrage.

a: The terror of the Lord was on all the cities around Shechem
p: This verse follows Genesis 35:5, where "a terror from God" kept the cities from chasing Jacob's sons.
b: Genesis 35:5 comes after God tells Jacob to go to Bethel: "a terror from God fell on the cities around them, so that no one chased the sons of Jacob." Jubilees moves it to the end of the Shechem story, as God's answer to Jacob's fear (30:25). Similar terror falls on Israel's enemies in Exodus 15:16 and Joshua 2:9.

a: Make yourselves clean and change your clothes
p: Jacob's call follows Genesis 35:1–4. In Genesis God tells him to go; here Jacob himself decides.
b: Genesis 35:1 begins with God's command: "Get up, go up to Bethel, and live there." Jubilees has no command; Jacob goes to keep the vow he made when he fled (27:27). His words follow Genesis 35:2–3: put away foreign gods, purify yourselves, change clothes. Washing and clean clothes before meeting God recall Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:10).

a: what was in their ears and on their necks
p: Genesis 35:4 mentions only rings in their ears. Charles suspected "necks" was a slip for "hands."
b: Genesis 35:4 says they handed over the foreign gods "in their hands, and the rings in their ears." Earrings and pendants were often charms or carried images of gods (compare Hosea 2:13). The Ge'ez says "in their ears and on their necks." Charles thought kəsawdihomu, "their necks," was a slip for "their hands," as in Genesis. VanderKam keeps "necks," and so does the Plain English Translation.
orig: ወዘውስተ እዘኒሆሙ ወዘውስተ ክሳውዲሆሙ (wäzäwsətä ʾəzänihomu wäzäwsətä kəsawdihomu)

a: He burned them, broke them to pieces and destroyed them
t: Compared with the Bible: the idols destroyed
p: In Genesis Jacob only hides the idols under the oak. Jubilees has him burn and break them first.
b: Genesis 35:4: "Jacob hid them under the oak that is by Shechem." Jubilees adds that he burned, broke and destroyed them, as the law later commands Israel to do with the nations' images: "burn their carved images" (Deuteronomy 7:5). The idols "that Rachel had stolen from Laban her father" are Laban's household gods (Genesis 31:19, 34). Goes beyond Genesis.

a: On the first day of the seventh month he went up to Bethel
p: Jacob reaches Bethel on the first day of the seventh month, a holy day in Leviticus and a memorial day in Jubilees.
b: Leviticus 23:24 makes the first day of the seventh month "a day of rest, a reminder made with loud blasts." It is also one of the four memorial days of Jubilees 6:23. Chapter 32 continues the story in this month: Jacob gives his tithe on the fourteenth (32:2) and brings burnt offerings on the fifteenth (32:4), the day Leviticus 23:34 makes the start of the Feast of Booths. So the trip to Bethel leads into the holiest month of the year.

a: He took two of his sons with him, Levi and Judah
t: Levi and Judah, priest and ruler
p: Genesis has no such visit. Syncellus quotes a Greek form of it, blessing Levi as high priest and Judah as king.
b: Genesis records no visit of Jacob to his parents with two of his sons. Charles notes that the visit is "unknown to later haggada," but that Syncellus quotes, under Josephus's name, a Greek summary: Isaac "blessed Levi as high priest and Judah as king and ruler." The Testament of Levi 9 also tells of the visit and says Isaac would not go to Bethel. Choosing these two sons points ahead to the two offices in Israel: priesthood and kingship.

a: her spirit came back to life
p: The same words are used of Jacob when he hears that Joseph is alive (Genesis 45:27).
b: When Jacob's sons tell him that Joseph lives, "their father Jacob's spirit lived again" (Genesis 45:27). Charles notes the parallel. By the book's dates Rebekah has not seen Jacob for nearly thirty years (27:19; 30:1), and in Genesis she never sees him again after he leaves. Jubilees gives mother and son a reunion.

a: The darkness left Isaac's eyes
t: Compared with the Bible: Isaac sees again
p: Isaac had grown blind (Genesis 27:1). Jubilees says his sight came back to see his grandsons.
b: Genesis 27:1 says Isaac's eyes "had grown too dim to see," and Jubilees agrees (26:1). Here the darkness passes and he sees Levi and Judah, then blesses them. The scene echoes Jacob's blessing of Joseph's sons, when Jacob's own eyes were dim (Genesis 48:10–14). Goes beyond Genesis.

a: A spirit of prophecy came down into his mouth
p: Isaac blesses by the spirit of prophecy, as Rebekah did (25:14). Hebrews calls his blessing an act of faith.
b: Charles links this verse with 25:14, where a spirit of righteousness comes down into Rebekah's mouth.
