In Genesis, Isaac's blessing reaches the future (Hebrews 11:20: "By faith Isaac gave Jacob and Esau a blessing that reached even to things still to come"). Isaac takes Levi by his right hand, the place of honor (compare Genesis 48:13–14).

a: He turned to Levi first
t: Compared with the Bible: Levi before Judah
p: In Genesis 49 Judah receives the scepter and Levi a curse. Here Levi is blessed first, as priest.
b: Jacob's blessing in Genesis 49 condemns Levi with Simeon (Genesis 49:5–7) and gives Judah the scepter (Genesis 49:10). Jubilees reverses the emphasis: Levi is blessed first, with priesthood, rule and teaching (31:13–17), then Judah with rule (31:18–20). Charles saw in the priest who also rules a picture of the early Maccabean (Hasmonean) priest-princes. The Testament of Levi 9 also has Isaac bless Levi. Goes beyond Genesis, and reverses its order of honor.

a: like the angels of the presence and like the holy ones
p: Levi's sons will serve in God's sanctuary as the highest angels serve in heaven.
b: The angels of the presence (mälaʾkətä gäṣ) are the highest angels, who narrate this book. Charles notes that "the holy ones" here seem to be a separate class. Malachi says of the priest, "for he is the messenger of the LORD of Armies" (Malachi 2:7), using the Hebrew word that means both "messenger" and "angel." Jubilees takes the comparison literally: Levi's line serves God as the angels do (compare 30:18).
orig: ከመ መላእክተ ገጽ ወከመ ቅዱሳን (kämä mälaʾkətä gäṣ wäkämä qədusan)

a: They will be rulers, princes and chiefs
p: Levi's sons will rule as well as serve. Charles read this as the early Maccabean priest-princes.
b: The blessing gives Levi's line two roles: to rule ("rulers, princes and chiefs") and to teach and bless as priests. Charles argued that this double role, "combined with other facts peculiar to the Maccabean period," points to the early Hasmonean princes, who were high priests and rulers at once. He compares the Testament of Levi 8, "high priests and judges and scribes." "Rulers" (mäkʷännən) is built on the same letters as yəkʷennu, "they will judge," later in the verse; Charles renders the title "judges." The Plain English Translation says "rulers" because the title here is about governing, as when Judah is made mäkʷännən in 31:18. On "chiefs" and the Latin, see the variant.

a: They will tell my ways to Jacob
p: The words echo Moses' blessing of Levi: "They will teach your rulings to Jacob" (Deuteronomy 33:10).
b: Moses blessed Levi: "They will teach your rulings to Jacob / and your law to Israel" (Deuteronomy 33:10). Malachi says "people look to his mouth for teaching" (Malachi 2:7). The last line, "The blessing of the Lord will be given in their mouth," recalls the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:23–27, and Charles compares Sirach 50:20, where the high priest blesses the people. The "my" in "my ways" is in the Ge'ez: for a moment God speaks through Isaac.

a: and rightly she called your name
p: Levi's name sounds like the Hebrew for "be joined." Leah named him hoping Jacob would be joined to her.
b: Leah named Levi saying, "This time, now, my husband will join himself to me" (Genesis 29:34). Numbers plays on the same word for the tribe: "They will be joined to you and serve you" (Numbers 18:2). Jubilees gives the name a higher sense: Levi "will be joined to the Lord." Charles points out the wordplay and notes that the Latin instead reads "for the beauty of God," linking the name to a Hebrew word for "garland."

a: Let his table be yours
p: Priests ate from the offerings brought to God's altar. Charles compares the Testament of Levi 8.
b: Priests lived from the offerings: "the holy gifts" were their share (Numbers 18:8–19; Deuteronomy 18:1–5). Paul uses the custom: "those who attend the altar have their share from the altar" (1 Corinthians 9:13). Charles compares the Testament of Levi 8, where Levi's offspring will share "the table of the Lord," and the Testament of Judah 21. Malachi uses "the LORD's table" for the altar (Malachi 1:7, 12).
r: Numbers 18:8–19; Deuteronomy 18:1–5; 1 Corinthians 9:13; Malachi 1:7; Testament of Levi 8

a: Be a ruler, you and one of your sons, over Jacob's sons
t: One of Judah's sons: a messiah?
p: Charles read "you and one of your sons" as the Messiah from Judah. Christians see Jesus, "out of Judah."
b: Genesis 49:10 promised that "The scepter will not leave Judah." Jubilees blesses Judah with rule, "you and one of your sons." Charles thought these words "admit most naturally" of a Messiah from Judah, and noted that other writings of the period look for a priestly leader from Levi (Testament of Levi 18) or a king from Judah (Testament of Judah 24). Others read "one of your sons" as David's line in general. Christians see the hope fulfilled in Jesus: "Everyone knows our Lord sprang up out of Judah" (Hebrews 7:14), who is also priest (Hebrews 7:15–17).
r: Genesis 49:10; Testament of Judah 24; Testament of Levi 18; Hebrews 7:14–17; Revelation 5:5

a: In you will be the help of Jacob
t: Judah, the help and salvation of Israel
p: Judah's line will bring Israel help and salvation, the role of the king from David's house.
b: The prophets promise a king from Judah who will save Israel: "In his days Judah will be saved" (Jeremiah 23:6; compare Jeremiah 33:16), and Zechariah 9:9 pictures the king who "is righteous, and he has been rescued." Jubilees gives Judah's line the work of help and salvation and Levi's line the work of teaching and blessing. Zechariah's song in Luke praises God, who "has raised up for us a horn of salvation" (Luke 1:69).

a: the throne of the honor of your righteousness
p: Charles reports that his manuscripts differ here. VanderKam's text is translated as it stands.
b: Charles reports that manuscript d reads "the throne of the honour of thy righteousness, there will be great peace," while b and c read "the throne of honour, thy righteousness will be great peace." The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's Ge'ez, which can be read the first way. Righteousness and peace together mark the reign of the coming king in Isaiah 9:7 and Psalm 72:1–7.

a: He came out from between his feet
p: The verse does not say who "came out from between his feet" and bowed.
b: The verse does not name who "came out from between his feet" and bowed: it may be Judah, kneeling at Isaac's feet, or Jacob. Charles thought "And he blessed them" seems "out of place here." The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez order and leaves "he" open. On a possible echo of Genesis 49:10, see Claude's note on this verse.

a: He came out from between his feet
t: Claude's theory: an echo of Genesis 49:10?
p: Claude's theory: "from between his feet" right after Judah's blessing may echo Genesis 49:10.
b: This is Claude's theory. Genesis 49:10 promises that "the ruler's staff" will not leave Judah "from between his feet." Here the same phrase follows Isaac's blessing of Judah, who is made a ruler (31:18). If the author had Genesis 49:10 in mind, the one who comes out "from between his feet" may be Judah. Charles does not draw this link, and I have not found it in the sources opened for this part.

a: it was counted to him as righteousness
p: The formula used of Levi's zeal (30:17) is used of Isaac's love for his grandsons.
b: Isaac lets his two grandsons sleep at his right and left, and "it was counted to him as righteousness." The formula comes from Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 106:31 and appears in this part of the book for Levi's zeal (30:17), Levi's whole life (30:20), and here for a grandfather's tenderness. In Jubilees righteousness is a record of deeds kept in heaven.

a: I am a hundred and sixty-five years old
p: Isaac cannot go to Bethel. The Testament of Levi 9 also says he would not go with them.
b: Genesis says Isaac lived to 180 (Genesis 35:28). In Jubilees he is 165 here and sends Rebekah with Jacob instead. Charles notes that the Testament of Levi 9 says the same of Isaac: "he would not go with us to Bethel." Riding on a donkey was the usual way for the old, women and travelers to journey (Genesis 22:3; 1 Samuel 25:20).

a: Do not put off your vow
p: Isaac urges Jacob to pay his vow quickly, as the law and Ecclesiastes teach.
b: Deuteronomy 23:21 says that when you make a vow to the LORD, you must not delay paying it, because God will require it of you. Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 gives the same advice. Isaac says Jacob "will be called to account for the vow," an echo of the same law. Jacob pays it in chapter 32 with the tenth of all he has.

a: and Deborah with her
p: Deborah came with Rebekah from Haran (Genesis 24:59). Genesis 35:8 says she died and was buried at Bethel.
b: Genesis names Rebekah's nurse only at her death: "Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried below Bethel under the oak" (Genesis 35:8). Genesis 24:59 mentions the nurse who came with Rebekah. Jubilees explains why Deborah was at Bethel: she came with Rebekah on this visit. Her death follows in chapter 32.

a: I have an eternal hope
t: Compared with the Bible: an eternal hope
p: Jacob speaks of "an eternal hope" for himself and his sons, words Genesis never uses.
b: The Ge'ez täsfa zäläʿaläm means "hope of eternity." In this book the hope is tied to the blessings written on the heavenly tablets, which last forever. The New Testament speaks of "the hope of eternal life" (Titus 1:2). Jubilees does not say clearly what Jacob hopes for beyond his sons' future; compare its picture of the righteous dead in 23:31. Goes beyond Genesis.
